title: Chapter 135 — Internal Communication
intro: Great customer service starts behind the counter.

sections.title: The Sales-to-Delivery Handoff
sections.content:
The most dropped ball in appliance retail is the gap between what the salesperson promised and what the delivery ticket says. The salesperson promised white-glove install with waterline hookup. The delivery ticket says 'drop at door.' The customer is furious and the delivery crew has no idea what was sold.

Every promise made during the sale must be documented on the delivery ticket. Installation type — basic connect, professional install, or no install. Haul-away — yes or no, and the location of the old unit. Special instructions — basement delivery, narrow hallway, elevator required. Accessories included — stacking kit, water line, vent kit, anti-tip bracket. Customer expectations — anything promised during the sale that is not standard.

If it is not on the ticket, it does not happen. Period. Treat the delivery ticket as a contract between you and the operations team.

sections.title: Leaving Notes That Help
sections.content:
CRM notes should help the next person who touches this customer, not just check a box for your manager.

Bad note: 'Spoke to customer.' Good note: 'Customer choosing between Bosch 500 and 800 series dishwashers. Main concern is drying performance. Husband prefers 500 for budget, wife wants 800 for CrystalDry. Follow up Thursday after they discuss.'

The second note lets any rep pick up the conversation seamlessly if you are off the floor. The first note is useless — it tells the next person nothing about where the sale stands, what the customer cares about, or what the next step is.

Write notes as if you will be out sick tomorrow and someone else has to take over your pipeline. Because someday you will be, and they will.

sections.title: Never Throw Coworkers Under the Bus
sections.content:
The customer does not need to know about internal disagreements, scheduling conflicts, or who made the mistake. They need to know it is being fixed.

'I am sorry about the confusion — let me sort this out for you right now.' Not: 'Yeah, the delivery team messed that up.' Not: 'That was the other rep who wrote up your order.' Own the resolution on behalf of the team, regardless of whose fault it was.

The customer's trust is in your store, not just in you. When you blame a colleague, you damage the store's credibility — and your own. The professional response is always to own the fix, not assign the blame.
